To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we report a quantitative method to measure protein-protein and peptide-protein interactions that uses only 1-2 mg of protein and requires no special instrumentation.

we have developed a quantitative, non-immobilization-based, non-surface-based, and non-instrumentation-based method for the analysis of the equilibrium dissociation constants and stoichiometry for protein-protein and peptide-protein complexes.
nickel-catalysed proximity biotinyling and Ru(II) (bpy)(3) (2+) mediated oxidative crosslinking are useful for the quantitative analysis of protein complexes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new methods to study protein interactions.
the development of chemical tools to quantitatively study protein-protein and peptide-protein interactions in vitro and in vivo.
the development of new synthetic strategies to control the reactivity of small molecules and the use of these methods in the quantitative analysis of protein complexes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the use of Ru(II) (bpy)(3) (2+)-mediates oxidative crosslinking, and Ni(II) (2,2'-bipyridine) catalyzed biotinylation, can provide a useful complement for the quantitative analysis of protein complexes.

the use of oxidative crosslinking chemistry in combination with biotinylation is a very powerful and sensitive tool to quantitatively determine protein-protein and peptide-protein interactions in solution.

the method described herein provides an easy-to-use and inexpensive approach for the quantitative characterization of protein interactions in a wide variety of systems, including those that are not amenable to analysis by other methods.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we developed a new chemistry for the quantitative analysis of protein complexes.
we have developed a new method for measuring protein-protein and peptide-protein interactions.
we can use these two methods to measure the equilibrium constants of protein complexes and the stoichiometry of the complexes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can use these two chemistries to quantify protein-protein complexes.

the chemistry of Ru(II)(byy)(3)(2+) and Ni(II) complexes can be used to quantitatively analyze the stoichiometry and equilibrium dissociation constants of protein complexes, and that the chemistry is compatible with the use of mass spectrometry to identify the crosslinked species.
we can use a combination of proximity biotiny and oxidative cross-linking chemistry to quantify protein-protein and peptide interactions in solution.
